newsitem.title: UK: UK business wary of continued sterling strength.
newsitem.headline: UK business wary of continued sterling strength.

text.p: British companies, fearing a dent in their competitive edge, are keeping a wary eye on sterling's relentless rally although currency hedging should limit the damage in the short-term, company spokesmen said.

With a British base rate rise looking increasingly likely, the pound soared to a 33-month peak against the mark on Friday, and prompted concern from some companies and employers' associations that exports could plummet.
"It's obviously bad for UK Plc," said Gordon Campbell, chief executive at chemicals company Courtaulds Plc. "It means the UK is less competitive."
"The extent of the rise in sterling is clearly a concern for industry," said Stephen Davies, economic research executive at the Institute of Directors.

Treasurers, finance directors and executives contacted by Reuters said their companies had undertaken hedging strategies to limit the near-term damage of currency wobbles. But exposure worries would persist if the rally were to continue through next year.

"We run foreign currency hedging up to 12 months forward...For the first half of next year we're still immune, but by the second half, we'll be fully exposed," said Angus Russell, group treasurer at British pharmaceutical and chemical firm Zeneca Group plc.

"All companies take action to hedge their positions as an ongoing process, but clearly if sterling strength is sustained, no matter what hedging is undertaken, it will catch up with you," said Richard Harris, head of taxation and treasury at auto components giant GKN Plc.

An increase in sterling relative to other currencies makes British goods more expensive abroad which lowers demand. By the same token imports are cheaper, producing an overall negative effect on British competitiveness.

So company executives, particularly in those firms where exports account for a large proportion of sales, are continuing to keep an eye on sterling, wary that there could be an adverse impact on the balance sheet if these levels are sustained.

"Around 94 percent of our sales are outside the UK so we are very sensitive to currency fluctuations," said Zeneca's Russell. "When sterling moves by five percent, we estimate it costs us 70-80 million sterling ($118-134 million) in pre-tax profit as a rule of thumb."
Sterling has put on 13 percent against the dollar since May, and looks like maintaining its dizzy heights for the foreseeable future.

"Assuming that the (sterling/mark) exchange rate is 2.50...the annual negative impact on British Steel is estimated by analysts to be something over 200 million sterling," a British Steel spokesman said, adding that the company was accelerating efficiency improvements to maintain its competitive edge.

In the near term, small- and medium-sized enterprises could struggle, hampered by a lack of experience and restricted access to those types of hedging strategies available to larger, more established firms.

"Many of our firms have developed a very solid export business but over a relatively short period. With the present strength of sterling this is proving a bit of a problem because companies need to maintain and sustain their export position," said David Botterill, chief executive of West Midlands Engineering and Employers Association.
"A company that has been operating on an international basis for 10 to 15 years is in a slightly different position. It is more able to adjust to the pulls and pushes of currencies," he added.
The pound traded at 2.5831/36 marks and 1.6830/40 dollars at 1110 GMT on Friday, and was at 94.1 on a trade-weighted basis.
On May 1 this year, sterling touched a two-year low against the dollar at 1.4888. At the beginning of August the pound was at 2.2765 marks.
